title: Prioritisation, delegation and accountability
blurb: Prioritise a group of patients, delegate safely within competence with clear instructions, and know who is accountable for what.
question: A registered nurse asks a healthcare assistant to take a patient's observations. The patient's blood pressure falls but the assistant does not report it. Who is accountable for what?

teach.body: Delegation is allocating a task to a competent person while you keep overall responsibility for the person's care. Accountability means being answerable for your actions and able to explain the judgement behind them. The registrant who delegates is accountable for the decision to delegate; the person who accepts a task is accountable for how they carry it out. In plain English: you can hand over the task, but not your responsibility for choosing the right person and checking the result.
teach.cite: NMC Code 11; RCN Accountability and delegation

teach.h: Code 11: be accountable for your decisions to delegate
items: 11.1 Delegate only tasks and duties within the other person's scope of competence, making sure they fully understand your instructions.
11.2 Make sure everyone you delegate to is adequately supervised and supported to provide safe and compassionate care.
11.3 Confirm that the outcome of any task you have delegated meets the required standard.

children.label: Do it yourself or find a competent person

teach.caption: Delegation must be in the person's best interests, not simply to save time or money (RCN).
Annexe A 4.1.2: clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating.

rows.label: Accountable for
values: Decision to delegate; supervision; checking outcome
How they carry out the task

rows.label: Must
values: Accept only what they are competent to do

rows.label: If unsure
values: Do the task or get a competent person

teach.caption: Nursing associates are NMC registrants bound by the Code; healthcare assistants are accountable to their employer and the law.

head: Role
Key points
rows: Assesses, plans, evaluates; delegates and supervises
NMC registrant (England); follows the Code; does not prescribe
Not registered; trained tasks in job description, with protocols
Learns under supervision; not counted as staff
teach.caption: Support workers should have clear guidelines so they are not required to make a standalone clinical judgement (RCN).

teach.body: When several patients need you at once, deal first with threats to life: airway, breathing and circulation problems, and high or rising NEWS2 scores. NEWS2 of 7 or more needs an emergency response; 5 to 6 or a single parameter scoring 3 needs urgent review. Next come time-critical care (for example a hypoglycaemia below 4.0 mmol/L, antibiotics in suspected sepsis), then routine care. Delegate appropriate tasks so nothing waits that need not.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Tariq on a busy late shift
teach.body: Tariq has four calls at once. Mr Ross has a NEWS2 of 7, so Tariq goes to him and calls for help. He asks Kim, a healthcare assistant trained in observations, to record Mrs Lee's observations now: 'Please do Mrs Lee's full set at 15:00 and tell me straight away if her systolic is under 100 or her pulse over 110.' Kim repeats it back. Later Tariq checks Kim's readings, signs the chart and gives Mrs Shah her routine medicines.

teach.text: Delegating a task does not delegate your accountability for the decision. If the person was not competent, or you did not check the outcome, the decision is yours to answer for.

items: Delegate within competence and role, with instructions they fully understand (Code 11.1).
Supervise and support (11.2) and confirm the outcome meets the standard (11.3).
The delegator is accountable for the decision; the person accepting is accountable for how they do it.
Delegation must be in the patient's interest, with protocols so support workers are not left to make clinical judgements alone.
Prioritise threats to life first (ABCDE, NEWS2), then time-critical care, then routine tasks.

summary: You can now prioritise care for a group of patients using ABCDE and NEWS2, delegate within competence with clear instructions and checked understanding, and explain who is accountable for the decision to delegate and for the task itself.

A.q: After delegating a wound dressing to a nursing associate, what does Code 11.3 require of the registered nurse?
options: Repeat the dressing herself to make sure
Confirm the outcome meets the standard
Countersign the nursing associate's notes
Report the task to the ward manager today
A.why: Code 11.3: confirm that the outcome of any task you have delegated to someone else meets the required standard.

whyNot.0: Redoing the task is unnecessary if the outcome meets the standard.
whyNot.2: Nursing associates are registrants who record their own care; countersigning is not what 11.3 requires.
whyNot.3: Routine delegated care does not need reporting to the manager.

A.q: Which instruction to a healthcare assistant best meets Annexe A 1.11 (clear verbal instructions when delegating)?
options: 'Keep a close eye on Mr Okafor for me all afternoon, please.'
'Do Mr Okafor's obs when you have a minute.'
'BP at 14:00, please; tell me now if systolic is under 100.'
'Let me know if Mr Okafor seems any worse to you later.'
A.why: A clear delegated instruction says what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when, removing ambiguity (AnnexA.1.11; AnnexA.4.1.2; Code 11.1).

whyNot.0: 'Keep an eye on' does not say what to check or what to report.
whyNot.1: No time or reporting threshold is given.
whyNot.3: 'Seems worse' leaves the assistant to make an unsupported clinical judgement.

A.q: A healthcare assistant says she has not been trained to check capillary blood glucose. The nurse had asked her to do it. What should the nurse do?
options: Talk her through it on the ward this time
Ask her to try it and record the result
Ask the patient to do the check for her
Do it herself or ask a trained colleague
A.why: Code 11.1: delegate only within the other person's scope of competence. A person asked to do something they are not trained for should say no, and the nurse does it or finds a competent person. Training can be arranged later (RCN).

whyNot.0: Talking someone through an untrained task does not make them competent.
whyNot.1: Trying an untrained task risks inaccurate results and harm.
whyNot.2: The patient's ability is a separate question; the nurse remains responsible for the check.

B.q: A nurse starts a late shift. Which patient should she see first?
options: Mr Hall, waiting for his discharge letter
Mrs Ford, asking for help to the bathroom
Mr Dee, NEWS2 7, newly confused
Ms Ray, routine 4-hourly observations due
B.why: A NEWS2 of 7 or more needs an emergency response and new confusion scores 3 on its own; this is potential life-threatening deterioration (NEWS2, RCP 2017; P5.5).

whyNot.0: A discharge letter is important but not urgent compared with deterioration.
whyNot.1: Help to the bathroom can be delegated to a competent HCA.
whyNot.3: Routine observations can be delegated or done after the emergency.

B.q: Priti, a registered nurse, delegates a dressing to Dean, a nursing associate. The dressing is applied incorrectly. Who is accountable for what?
options: Priti for delegating; Dean for doing it
Priti for everything, as she delegated it
Dean for everything, as he did the dressing
The ward manager, who sets the off-duty rota
B.why: The delegating registrant is accountable for the decision to delegate and for checking the outcome; Dean, as an NMC registrant bound by the Code, is accountable for how he carried out the task (Code 11; RCN).

whyNot.1: Dean is a registrant and accountable for his own practice.
whyNot.2: Priti remains accountable for the decision to delegate and confirming the outcome.
whyNot.3: The ward manager has organisational responsibilities but not for this individual decision.

B.q: A nurse plans to delegate several tasks to a healthcare assistant mainly so she can leave on time. Which principle of delegation does this risk breaching?
options: Delegation must be to a registered professional
Delegation must be documented in the medical notes
Delegation must be agreed by the patient's family
Delegation must be in the patient's best interests
B.why: Delegation must be in the best interests of the person receiving care and not done simply to save time or money (RCN Accountability and delegation; Code 11).

whyNot.0: Tasks can be delegated to competent unregistered staff such as HCAs.
whyNot.1: Documentation of care matters, but this is not the principle at risk here.
whyNot.2: Family agreement is not a requirement for delegating tasks.

C.q: Grace has three patients needing her at once: Mrs Bell, sweaty with capillary glucose 3.1 mmol/L and able to swallow; Mr Shaw, IV antibiotics due in 30 minutes; Mr Cole, asking for a wash. What is the best plan?
options: Give the antibiotics first, then treat Mrs Bell
Treat Mrs Bell now; a trained HCA helps Mr Cole
Wash Mr Cole first, as he was the first to ask
Ask the HCA to treat Mrs Bell while she does the IV
C.why: Mrs Bell is hypoglycaemic (below 4.0 mmol/L) and needs fast-acting glucose now (RCUK first aid). The antibiotics are due in 30 minutes and can follow. The wash can be delegated to a competent HCA (P5.5; Code 11.1).

whyNot.0: The antibiotics are not yet due, while hypoglycaemia needs treating now.
whyNot.2: Order of asking does not set clinical priority.
whyNot.3: Treating and reassessing hypoglycaemia needs registered oversight; the wash is the task to delegate.

C.q: A second-year student nurse offers to do the lunchtime medicines round alone because the ward is short-staffed. What should the registered nurse do?
options: Accept, as the student is in her second year
Accept, if the student signs each chart entry
Ask the HCA to check the student's round
Supervise the student giving the medicines
C.why: Students are supernumerary and learn under supervision; they are not used to fill a staffing gap. The registrant supervises the student's medicines administration at the level local policy and the student's learning needs require, and remains accountable (Code 11.1–11.2; NMC SSSA).

whyNot.0: Year of study does not make a supernumerary student a substitute for a missing registrant on the round.
whyNot.1: Signing the chart does not provide the supervision required.
whyNot.2: An HCA cannot supervise medicines administration.

C.q: A nurse wants a healthcare assistant to help monitor Mr Price, who has PRN analgesia prescribed. Which delegated instruction is appropriate?
options: 'Decide if he needs his PRN and let me know after.'
'Give him a PRN dose if he looks uncomfortable.'
'Ask his pain score hourly; tell me if it is 4+.'
'Watch him and use your judgement about pain relief.'
C.why: Delegated tasks need clear protocols so support workers are not required to make a standalone clinical judgement (RCN). A defined task with a reporting threshold keeps the clinical decision with the nurse (AnnexA.1.11).

whyNot.0: Deciding on PRN medicine is a clinical judgement for the registrant.
whyNot.1: Administering a PRN dose on appearance is outside an HCA's role and competence.
whyNot.3: 'Use your judgement' leaves the HCA to make a clinical decision alone.

reteach.title: Passing the baton, keeping the race
reteach.question: In a relay, the runner hands over the baton. Who chose the next runner, and who must watch the handover?

blocks.body: Delegation is like a relay handover. The task (the baton) passes to someone else, who is responsible for running their leg well. But you chose them, so you must be sure they can run it, tell them clearly where to go, watch the handover and check they finished. If you picked someone who had never trained, the choice is yours to answer for.

blocks.h: A memory aid (not an official tool): RIGHT

letters.word: Right task: in the patient's interest

blocks.text: The person accepting a task can and should say no if they are not competent. That protects the patient; it is not unhelpfulness.

explain.body: 11.1 within competence, instructions understood; 11.2 supervised and supported; 11.3 confirm the outcome meets the required standard.

test.q: Which part of the Code says to delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence?
options: Code 11.1
Code 13.3
Code 16.2
Code 25.2
test.why: Code 11.1: only delegate tasks and duties that are within the other person's scope of competence, making sure that they fully understand your instructions.

whyNot.1: Code 13.3 is about asking for help when something is beyond your own competence.
whyNot.2: Code 16.2 is about raising concerns if asked to practise beyond your role.
whyNot.3: Code 25.2 is about supporting staff to follow the Code.

explain.body: Say what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when. Check understanding by asking the person to repeat it back (AnnexA.4.1.2).

test.q: After giving a healthcare assistant instructions, what is the best way for the nurse to check understanding?
options: Ask 'Is that OK?'
Ask her to repeat the plan back
Write it in the nursing notes now
Repeat it more slowly
test.why: Asking the person to repeat back the task and reporting thresholds confirms understanding (AnnexA.4.1.2; Code 11.1 'fully understand your instructions').

whyNot.0: A yes/no question often gets 'yes' without real understanding.
whyNot.2: Documentation does not check that she has understood.
whyNot.3: Repeating it does not show whether she understood.

explain.body: The delegator is accountable for the decision to delegate, supervision and checking the outcome. The person accepting is accountable for how they do it, and should decline tasks they are not competent to do.

test.q: What should a healthcare assistant do if asked to carry out a task she has not been trained to do?
options: Explain she is not trained and decline
Do it carefully and ask afterwards
Ask another assistant to do it instead
Watch a video and then attempt it
test.why: The person accepting a task must be competent to do it; if not, they should say no and explain why (RCN Accountability and delegation).

whyNot.1: Attempting an untrained task risks harm to the patient.
whyNot.2: Passing it to another untrained colleague does not resolve the problem.
whyNot.3: A video does not provide assessed competence.

explain.body: Threats to life first (ABCDE, NEWS2 7+ or rising, single parameter 3), then time-critical care, then routine tasks, delegating what is safe to delegate.

test.q: Which finding should a nurse act on first when allocating her time?
options: A request for a cup of tea
A routine medicine due in an hour
A NEWS2 score of 7
A relative wanting an update
test.why: NEWS2 of 7 or more is a high clinical risk needing an emergency response (RCP 2017).

whyNot.0: A drink request can be delegated.
whyNot.1: A medicine due in an hour is not as urgent as possible critical illness.
whyNot.3: Updating relatives matters but can wait for the emergency.
